title: Will AI Leave You Behind? What Every Woman Needs to Know Now
guestBio: LaVada English is the Founder and CEO of Bright Places, Inc., a strategic coaching firm specializing in leadership development, team synergy, and AI leadership strategy. She is also the Co-Founder and Co-CEO of the National Association of Women in AI (NAWAI), an organization born from a 4 a.m. moment of clarity and 25+ years in talent development. LaVada is the author of Finding Peace in Chaos and Leading Through Change, and the mother of three daughters.
excerpt: AI isn't just a tech trend — it's a wealth event, and women are at the center of it whether they're ready or not. LaVada English, Co-Founder of the National Association of Women in AI, breaks down exactly why the gender wage gap could get worse before it gets better, and what non-technical women can do starting today to make sure they're on the right side of history.
metaDescription: LaVada English on why AI could widen the gender wage gap — and the practical, non-technical steps women can take right now to stay ahead.
keyTakeaways: You don't need a computer science degree to leverage AI — you need a deliberate strategy and the willingness to show up consistently, even if that's just one hour, three days a week.
The jobs most likely to be augmented or displaced by AI skew 60–70% toward roles women currently hold, making AI literacy a women's economic issue, not just a tech industry conversation.
Treat AI like a new hire, not a CEO — start it as an intern, give it context and guardrails, and only promote it to a leadership role in your workflow once it has earned your trust.

Certifications from the ecosystems your clients already live in — think Microsoft, Google, and Amazon — carry real résumé weight and signal to employers and clients that you're serious about staying current.
Hallucinations are a real risk, but they're easiest to catch in your own area of expertise, which is exactly why you should always ask AI for its source and never publish without verifying.

Never input sensitive client data, proprietary business information, or personally identifying details into a public AI tool — create a named persona (like 'Alex') to represent your business without exposing it.
Waiting for your company, your industry, or someone else to hand you an AI strategy is not a strategy — join at least three AI communities, show up, and build your own on-ramp.

content:
There is a wealth event happening right now, and most women don't know they're already in it. Artificial intelligence is not a future problem. It is not a tech-bro conversation you can afford to scroll past. It is reshaping who gets hired, who gets paid, and who gets left behind — and the data is not subtle about which direction women are trending.

In Episode 76 of The Manage Her® Podcast, Aimee sits down with LaVada English — Founder and CEO of Bright Places, Inc. and Co-Founder of the National Association of Women in AI (NAWAI) — for a conversation that manages to be both a wake-up call and a genuine on-ramp. LaVada has spent more than 25 years in talent development. She has seen workforce shifts come and go. And she is unambiguous: this one is different, and ignorance is not a strategy.

The 78-Cents Problem Is About to Get Worse

You already know the number. Women earn roughly 78 cents for every dollar a man earns. What you may not know is that the jobs most likely to be augmented — or outright replaced — by AI skew 60 to 70 percent toward roles women currently hold. Administrative work. Customer service. Data entry. Coordination. These are not low-skill jobs. They are jobs that women have built careers in, and they are directly in AI's crosshairs.

LaVada doesn't share this to frighten you. She shares it because the women who understand what's coming are the ones who get to shape it. "What will history say about us?" she asks — and it's the kind of question that doesn't let you go back to scrolling.

The 4 A.M. Moment That Started a Movement

NAWAI didn't begin in a boardroom with a pitch deck. It began at 4 a.m. during a hot flash, when LaVada sat up in bed and started doing math she couldn't stop doing. She looked at who was building AI. She looked at who was being displaced by it. And she recognized that the two groups barely overlapped — and that someone had to do something about the gap.

That someone turned out to be her. Twenty-five years of experience in talent development gave her both the vocabulary and the urgency to build something real. NAWAI launched as a national organization dedicated to equipping women with the literacy, community, and credentials to participate in — and lead — the AI economy. If that story doesn't move you a little, check your pulse.

You Don't Need to Be Technical. You Need to Be Strategic.

This is the part of the conversation that Aimee and LaVada return to again and again, because it is the myth that is doing the most damage. Women are opting out of AI literacy before they even begin, telling themselves some version of I'm not a tech person — as if the only path to relevance runs through a computer science degree.

It doesn't. LaVada's framework is disarmingly simple: treat AI like a new hire, not a CEO. You wouldn't hand a brand-new employee your most sensitive client relationships on day one. You would give them context. You would assign them tasks within their scope. You would evaluate their output before it went out the door. AI deserves exactly the same management philosophy — and if you've ever managed a person, you already have the skills to manage a tool.

The progression she teaches moves from Intern → Associate → Director → Executive. Start by giving AI the small, low-stakes tasks. Learn how it responds. Learn where it surprises you, where it disappoints you, and where it actually makes your work sharper. Promote it incrementally, as trust is earned — the same way you'd grow anyone on your team.

AI as Thought Partner, Not Thought Leader

One of the most important distinctions LaVada draws in this episode is the difference between using AI as a thought partner versus surrendering to it as a thought leader. A thought partner pushes your thinking, offers angles you hadn't considered, and helps you stress-test your ideas. A thought leader tells you what to think — and that role is yours alone.

This matters for your business. It matters for your children. LaVada is raising three daughters in the AI age, and she's intentional about teaching them that AI is a tool in service of their minds, not a replacement for developing one. The same lesson applies to you, no matter where you are in your career.

What You Should Never Put Into an AI Tool

LaVada is practical about risk in a way that most AI conversations skip over. Public-facing AI tools do not come with the privacy guarantees of your company's internal systems. That means client names, proprietary processes, personal identifying information, and sensitive business strategy have no business being typed into a general-purpose AI chatbot.

Her solution is elegant: create a named persona — she calls hers "Alex" — that represents your business in the abstract. Alex works in a specific industry, serves a specific kind of client, and has specific goals. When you prompt AI using Alex as the stand-in, you get the strategic value without exposing what actually matters. It's a small guardrail that professionals at every level can implement today.

Certifications That Actually Move the Needle

When it comes to credentials, LaVada is pointed: get certified in the ecosystems your clients already use. Microsoft. Google. Amazon. These are not vanity certificates. They signal to employers, clients, and collaborators that you have done the work — and they come from names that already have trust built into them. If you've been paralyzed by the overwhelming number of AI courses available, this is your shortcut to clarity.

Community Is the Strategy Nobody Talks About Enough

If there's one mandate that runs through this entire conversation, it's this: you cannot do this alone, and you shouldn't have to. LaVada's advice is to join at least three AI-focused communities — professional groups, online forums, organizations like NAWAI — and to show up in them consistently. Not to perform expertise you don't yet have, but to be in the room where the conversation is happening.

The women who are going to be on the right side of this economic shift are the ones who refused to wait for someone else to build their on-ramp. One hour. Three days a week. That's all it takes to stop falling behind — and it starts the moment you decide that waiting is no longer an option.

This episode will make you feel seen, challenged, and genuinely equipped. Whether you're a CEO, a mom returning to the workforce, or someone who has been quietly telling herself she's just not a tech person — LaVada English has something for you. And so does Aimee. Hit play.
